extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and critical thinking; scientific inquirers interested in methodological errors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying and avoiding a priori fallacies and related methodological errors in arguments about nature, metaphysics, and scientific law. Focuses on common mistaken principles by which thinkers infer facts from ideas, language, or lack of imagination rather than from experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid accepting propositions as self-evident without proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not embrace conclusions as proved merely because they are presented as requiring no proof or as self-evident; recognize that some propositions are alleged to be knowable a priori but may be improperly assumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cautions that although some ultimate premises must be accepted to avoid infinite regress, determining which premises legitimately require no proof is the central (metaphysical) problem. Practically, be wary of claims presented as 'requiring no proof' and scrutinize whether they rest on intuition or unsupported presumption rather than evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer objective reality from subjective ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid treating ideas, sensations, or mental conceptions as if they directly establish the existence or properties of external things — i.e., mistaking subjective facts for objective realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ontological school claims intuitive apprehension of realities; opponents see this as finding an idea in the mind and inferring an external reality. The fallacy consists in attributing properties of ideas (or laws of the mind) to objects themselves. Check whether purported 'intuitions' are just concept-contents rather than independent evidence of external facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association-to-coexistence fallacy (thinking together ⇒ existing together)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume that because two things are habitually thought of together they necessarily co-exist or are causally connected in reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Widely illustrated by superstitions and omens (e.g., 'talk of the devil and he will appear', unlucky days, auguries). Such associations can predispose perception (malobservation) and false generalization, producing beliefs that merely reflect psychological association rather than causal or factual links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconceivability does not imply impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: It is fallacious to assert that whatever we cannot conceive cannot be true; limits of human conception are not proof of limits in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: objections to antipodes, to the Copernican system, and Newton's initial incredulity at action at a distance. The passage warns that what seems inconceivable may reflect only our present imaginative limits and that future extension of experience can make formerly inconceivable combinations imaginable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual entailment fallacy (what is in the idea must exist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the assumption that whatever is 'involved in the idea' of a thing (or whatever we can distinctly conceive) must therefore exist in the object or in reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descartes' maxim ('whatever can be very clearly conceived must be true' when existence is 'involved in the idea') exemplifies this error. The passage explains that ideas contain only what has been put into them and that deriving existence from conceptual content leads to circular or question-begging reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favoring simplest or easiest-conceived hypotheses as likeliest
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not presume that the hypothesis which is easiest to conceive or simplest in form is most likely to be true (the naive 'nature acts by the simplest means' assumption).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically this led to persistent errors (e.g., insisting celestial motion be circular or explained by spheres). The text cautions against taking conceptual simplicity as a reliable guide to the truth of physical hypotheses without empirical support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misuse of the Principle of Sufficient Reason (no reason to the contrary ⇒ law holds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid arguing a law a priori on the ground that we see no reason for deviation; absence of an obvious reason is not proof that deviation cannot occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by attempted a priori proofs of inertia and the first law of motion (argument that without an external force there is no reason for motion in any particular direction). The critique shows such reasoning often begs the question (petitio principii) and that empirical evidence is the real test of laws of nature. Also discussed: the possibility of internal or asymmetric causes and the improper dismissal of alternatives because they seem arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reification / personification of abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat names of abstractions or general terms (e.g., 'Nature', 'Chance', 'Fate', 'Space', 'Time', 'man in general') as indicating distinct, separable entities with independent existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Called mysticism in the text: ascribing objective existence to subjective creations of the mind (e.g., universals as 'substances'). This leads to metaphysical confusion by positing spurious entities and diverting inquiry away from observable phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflating linguistic distinctions with natural distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of assuming that differences in common language or names correspond to real, ontological differences in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Greek philosophers' tendency to read metaphysical truths out of ordinary linguistic usages (e.g., different senses of 'in') exemplifies this error. Early science often erred by treating popular phrases or grammatical distinctions as if they demarcated natural kinds or laws. Scrutinize whether classificatory differences stem from language habits rather than empirical differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for clustering of fallacies that reinforce each other
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that multiple fallacies (e.g., malobservation, false generalization, unjustified a priori assumptions) often occur together and mutually reinforce erroneous beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: superstitions often combine association-to-coexistence, malobservation (seeing what one expects), and false generalization. When evaluating an argument, check for such clusters rather than treating apparent errors in isolation; one fallacy can smooth the way for others.
